title: Converting my Language Learning App to Spring Boot
content: This is the second part in a series where I build a language learning app using Java and Spring Boot. Please see this post for an overview of the project.  In the previous part of my LangLearner project, I constructed a console application in Java using domain-driven and test-driven design. In this part, I want to take some time to delve into the Spring framework and Spring Boot, and how it can help to make my application more robust.  Why use a framework?  As I understand it, frameworks encompass the ‘plumbing’ of an app: technical concerns such as handling HTTP requests, connecting to a database, security, or logging, which do not depend on the domain logic. Frameworks are widely employed in modern software engineering for a few reasons:     Frameworks save the developer the time and effort of building their own code structure.   Frameworks are less susceptible to bugs than custom code.   Because frameworks are widely adopted, they provide a common language between developers.   I won’t get into these reasons in detail; for that, I’m happy to refer to the wonderful Spring Start Here1. The better question for me at this time is: why do I want to use Spring for my project? That informs what aspects of the Spring framework I should look to.  In my case, there are two things I want to do with Spring:     Handing over initialization to Spring by using the Spring Core application context   Creating an API using Spring MVC   In this post, I will focus on the first part. The end product for this part will be a Spring Boot console application.  Adding Beans to Spring’s application context  To understand how Spring works, it helps to note that my ‘main function’ actually has two separate responsibilities. First, it instantiates the application, by creating a Deck connected to a Vocabulary. Second, it runs the application exactly once.  To make this separation more explicit, I can extract the functionality for running the application to a separate class, which I’ll call ConsoleSession.  public class ConsoleSession {     private final Deck deck;      public ConsoleSession(Deck deck) {         this.deck = deck;     }      public void run() {         //Draw cards until deck is exhausted.     } }   My LangLearnerConsole class now looks like this:  public class LangLearnerConsole {     public static void main(String [] args) {         ConsoleSession session = new ConsoleSession(Deck(Vocabulary("wordlist.txt")));         session.run();     } }   In the first line of my main function I instantiate my application, and in the second line I run it. Spring can augment both steps but for now, I will focus on the initialization step.  A foundational concept in the Spring framework is Inversion of Control (IoC). Inversion of control means that, instead of instantiating and connecting objects myself, I hand fine-grained control of select objects (called Beans) over to Spring. The basic structure of my main function then looks like this:  public class LangLearnerConsole {     public static void main(String [] args) {         var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(LangLearnerConsole.class);         context.getBean(ConsoleSession.class).run();     } }   Note that, in this new version, I’m not specifying any details about the application in the initialization step. This is by design: it prevents me from putting doman logic in the application’s main method. Instead, I tell Spring to initialize its application context.  Currently the application context is empty, so the application can’t run yet. If I request a Bean of type ConsoleSession, Spring will return an error. To make the application run, I need to make Spring aware of the required Beans.  There are multiple ways to add Beans to Spring’s application context, but an oft-preferred method is to use stereotype annotations. Stereotype annotations are added above class definitions, and tell Spring to create exactly one instance of that class. For example, I can add an instance of ConsoleSession to Spring’s application context by annotating it with @Component2.  @Component public class ConsoleSession {     private final Deck deck;      public ConsoleSession(Deck deck) {         this.deck = deck;     }      //Omitted ConsoleSession methods }   For Spring to instantiate a console session, it will also need a Deck. Again, I tell Spring to instantiate a Deck by annotating it with @Component.  @Component public class Deck{     private final IVocabulary vocabulary;     private Card drawnCard;      Deck(IVocabulary vocabulary) {         this.vocabulary = vocabulary;     }      //Omitted Deck methods }   I don’t need to annotate Card as a component, since I’m not using any of Spring’s functionalities for these. However, I am going to need an IVocabulary object in order to instantiate my Deck. To do that, I place a stereotype annotation above the TextVocabulary class. The interface itself is never annotated, since interfaces hold no meaning to Spring.  I annotate TextVocabulary with @Repository. This stereotype inherits from @Component, and therefore tells Spring to create exactly one instance of the class. However, using @Repository is preferable here because it also provides information about the role of TextVocabulary, both to Spring and to anyone reading the code.  @Repository public TextVocabulary implements IVocabulary {     //Omitted fields     public TextVocabulary(String filename) {        //Omitted file reading     }     //Omitted IVocabulary implementations }   Finally, I need to provide Spring with a filename for TextVocabulary to read out. I can’t use a stereotype annotation for this, since that would require me to directly modify the String class. Instead, I can manually create a @Bean of type String within my LangLearnerConsole class. I annotate LangLearnerConsole as a @Configuration to indicate that it can be a source of Beans. I also annotate it as @ComponentScan to make it look for stereotype annotations.  @Configuration @ComponentScan public class LangLearnerConsole {     public static void main(String [] args) {         var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(LangLearnerConsole.class);         context.getBean(ConsoleSession.class).run();     }      @Bean     public String filename() {         return "wordlist.txt";     } }   Now, Spring has enough information to construct its application context: it uses the filename I provided to instantiate a TextVocabulary, which it uses to instantiate a Deck, which in turn is used to instantiate a ConsoleSession. Note that I never explicitly specified how these objects should be connected; because the structure is so simple, Spring can ‘auto-wire’ the objects. For a more complex app this process, called dependency injection (DI), is more involved.  My console application runs now, but as a downside, the name of my vocabulary file is now hard-coded in this @Bean method. For the final part of this post, I will externalize my vocabulary file name by using Spring Boot and its application.properties file.  Externalizing my vocabulary file with Spring Boot  Spring Boot is a part of the Spring ecosystem, of which the core idea is ‘convention over configuration’. Spring itself offers extensive configuration options, but for many use cases, such customization is not necessary. Spring Boot provides many preconfigured functionalities which make it easier to set up a Spring application.  I will use two features offered by Spring Boot for my console application. Most importantly, I will use Spring Boot’s application.properties file to store my vocabulary file. I will also use Spring Boot’s CommandLineRunner interface to make my LangLearnerConsole class a little more concise.  In Spring Boot, application.properties is a standard file used for configuration. When I store the name of my vocabulary file in application.properties, I can directly access it in TextVocabulary:  vocabulary.filename: wordlist.txt   @Repository public TextVocabulary implements IVocabulary {     //Omitted fields     public TextVocabulary(@Value("${vocabulary.filename}") String filename) {        //Omitted file reading     }     //Omitted IVocabulary implementations }   To make use of application.properties and other Spring Boot features, I need to call the SpringApplication.run method, and add the @EnableAutoConfiguration annotation. Since the combination of @Configuration, @Componentscan and @EnableAutoConfiguration is used so often, Spring Boot lets me replace all of them by @SpringBootApplication.  In addition to using application.properties, I’ve also marked my ConsoleSession class as a CommandLineRunner. This is an interface provided by Spring Boot, which signals that arun method (with potential program arguments) should automatically be run when the CommandLineRunner is part of a Spring Boot application. That exactly fits the function which my ConsoleSession fulfills.  Thanks to these Spring Boot features, my LangLearnerConsole class now requires minimal information about the underlying application.  @SpringBootApplication public class LangLearnerConsole {      public static void main(String[] args) {         SpringApplication.run(LangLearnerConsole.class).close();     }  }   With this, I’ve successfully converted my console application to a Spring Boot application. The console output is the same as in the previous part, in essence, but it’s now surrounded by information provided by Spring Boot’s autoconfiguration. I can tell that the application is a Spring Boot application by its header:    .   ____          _            __ _ _  /\\ / ___'_ __ _ _(_)_ __  __ _ \ \ \ \ ( ( )\___ | '_ | '_| | '_ \/ _` | \ \ \ \  \\/  ___)| |_)| | | | | || (_| |  ) ) ) )   '  |____| .__|_| |_|_| |_\__, | / / / /  =========|_|==============|___/=/_/_/_/   :: Spring Boot ::                (v4.0.6)   The next step is to go from my current console application to a RESTful API, which I can use to build a web application. Spring Boot is especially useful for this, as I show in the next part.  Except where explicitly specified, generative AI was not used for this project.                 Laurenţiu Spilcă. Spring Start Here (2021). ↩︎                 In my actual code I use Controller rather than Component, but I prefer to get into this when I discuss my RESTful API in the next part. ↩︎

title: A Console App for Language Learning with Domain-Driven and Test-Driven Design
content: This is the first part in a series where I build a language learning app using Java and Spring Boot. Please see this post for an overview of the project.  In this first part of my LangLearner project, I will work out the design of my application. As already mentioned in the overview, I will be using test-driven design for this. In addition, I will use UML diagrams, specifically class and sequence diagrams, to visualize my design. The end product for this part is a console application in Java.  Building the domain model  The first step in building my language learning application is to ask what my domain logic is. In other words: how will my app help someone to learn vocabulary? A good way to figure this out is to pay close attention to the nouns and verbs that people are naturally inclined to use 1.  Traditionally, if I want to learn a language I might use a deck of flash cards. Whenever I draw a card, I read the front of the card, and try to translate the word. I then check whether my translation matches the back of the card, before moving on to the next card.  So I will need a Deck, which allows me to draw a Card from it. A Card has a front and a back. I need to be able to read the front, and check that my answer matches the back. I might want to add more functionalities, like shuffling the deck, or showing the correct answer to the user, but I think this is a good minimal model to start with.  To describe my Deck and Card objects I can draw a UML class diagram which looks something like this:    As you can see, my class diagram is closely tied to my description above. The only refinement I’ve made is that I’ve added a getter method, getDrawnCard. This method exists to avoid draw from taking on multiple responsibilities (modifying the deck, and returning a Card object).  There’s still one glaring issue that I’m left with here, though: where is the Deck coming from? The way it looks now, it seems as though I need to manually provide the cards property to the Deck. That might work for a few words, but it’s clearly not very convenient for a language learning app! I’ll get back to that, but before that, I will first implement these functions.  Implementing scenarios with test-driven design  As noted in my overview, I am applying test-driven design, which means I’m writing the tests for my classes and methods before I write their implementations. To know what tests I should write, I can consider the different scenarios which may occur:     The user draws a card and translates it correctly.   The user draws a card and translates it incorrectly.   There are no more cards remaining in the deck.   I can work out these three scenarios more fully using sequence diagrams. I’ll start with the scenario where there are no more cards remaining in the deck, since that is the simplest case. All I need to do is tell the user that they’re done.    Now for the scenario where the user successfully draws a card. I don’t think I need to distinguish between the cases where the user translates correctly or incorrectly, as the only difference between the two right now is in the feedback that the user receives. I end up with this sequence diagram:    Based on these sequence diagrams, I’ve written my tests and worked out my domain model. Again, I’m still creating my Deck manually, but for testing purposes this is not a problem.  The Repository pattern  I mentioned that it was not quite clear where the Deck was coming from. Now it’s time to address this point. For my original LangLearner program, I would simply have the program read out my vocabulary from two columns in a .txt file. I could do the same in my current model, by providing my Deck with a .txt file to read out.  However, I would prefer not to put the logic for reading out a file in the constructor of Deck. This would hide too much complexity in my Deck object, and muddle my design. It’s better to give the responsibility for reading out and storing vocabulary to a separate domain object, which I’ll call TextVocabulary.    This is already a lot better than what I had before. Now that TextVocabulary is responsible for reading out and storing vocabulary, I can keep Deck simple.  At the same time, I now have the issue that my Deck depends on TextVocabulary. This is a problem because TextVocabulary is not a part of my domain logic. As the app develops, I might want to store my vocabulary data in a different format like SQL or NoSQL (e.g., MongoDB). I don’t want to overhaul my entire design when I reach that point.  That’s where we get to the widely-used Repository pattern. The idea of the Repository pattern is that, no matter what is happening under the hood, it behaves as though all data were directly stored in memory 12. To achieve this, I can create an interface, which I call IVocabulary.    Thanks to this IVocabulary interface, it’s now clear where the boundary of my domain model lies: IVocabulary is a part of the domain, but its implementations, including TextVocabulary, are not.  Now, I want to emphasize that using a text file for the vocabulary is not necessarily a problem, especially for language learning! When I come across a new word while reading or listening, I don’t want to have to stop what I’m doing to put these words in a database. I just want to jot the word down and move on. That’s why, to this day, I still use those same text files to keep track of my vocabulary.  So it doesn’t have to be a bad thing that my ‘database’ just reads out a text file. It only becomes an issue when I’m tied down to it.  Building a console application  The first version of my app is almost complete now. I can create a Deck from a Vocabulary, draw Cards from the deck, read the words on the front of the cards, and check whether a given translation is correct. All that I need to do now is to put it all together. I could create a class with a main function which loops over the cards:   public class LangLearnerConsole {     public static void main(String @NonNull [] args) {         try  {             Deck deck = new Deck(new TextVocabulary(args[0]));              Scanner scn = new Scanner(System.in);             while (deck.draw()) {                 System.out.println("Translate: " + deck.readCard());                 String answer = scn.nextLine();                 if (deck.translateCard(answer)) {                     System.out.println("Correct!");                 }                 else {                     System.out.println("That is incorrect.");                 }             }             System.out.println("You have translated all words!");         } catch (IOException e) {             System.out.println("Could not find file.");         }     } }    This produces a working Java application, though a very simple one. As an example, I have an input called wordlist.txt, which contains two comma-separated columns of words, in English and Finnish respectively.  cat, kissa dog, koira bird, lintu bear, karhu  If I provide this file as an argument for my Java app, then it draws these cards in order, allows me to submit a translation, and gives me feedback:    As you can see, the application works as intended. Still, it’s not very satisfying. Even though I carefully constructed my domain model, I still have this vague ‘main function’ to worry about. So how can I improve on this process? Well, that’s where a framework like Spring comes in. I will discuss this in the next post.  The console app described in this post can be found here.  Except where explicitly specified, generative AI was not used for this project.  References  UML diagrams made using Excalidraw.                Eric Evans. Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software. ↩︎ ↩︎2                 Harry Percival & Bob Gregory. Architecture patterns with Python. ↩︎

title: Building a Language Learning App with Java and Spring Boot
content: When I was just starting to learn Python, I got the idea to use it to build a language learning application. The idea was simple: pick a word from a vocabulary list, ask the user to provide the translated word, and have the program check if the user is correct. To test the application, I used a short list of Finnish words, as I had had an interest in learning the language.  As it turns out, I would extensively use this program in my language learning journey. What I liked about it was that I could use my personal vocabulary list, and I didn’t need to put in any extra effort. Whenever I updated my vocabulary list with a new word, I could immediately use that. I also experimented with other features. The most important of these was a save function, as my vocabulary grew from a couple hundred to a couple thousand.  In the years since, I’ve been continuing to learn Finnish, yet my LangLearner application has grown somewhat neglected. That’s where this project comes in.  Overview     A Console App for Language Learning with Domain-Driven and Test-Driven Design   Converting my Language Learning App to Spring Boot   Goals My goal for this project is  to rebuild my LangLearner application from scratch, while sticking true to the spirit of the original program. While I originally used Python, for this new version I’ve chosen to use Java. It’s a language that I’ve been wanting to use more, and I think it is more natively suited for building applications than Python.  I’ve also been wanting to dip my toes into the Spring framework. I think LangLearner will be well-suited for that, as the appliciation itself is relatively simple, but at the same time it requires both a database and a user interface.  My goals are therefore as follows:     Build a domain in Java to pull pairs of words (‘flash cards’) from a deck, and check these against user input.   Have this domain comply with the Spring framework.   Build a database which can store custom vocabulary lists based on .txt files.   Implement a save/load function to deal with long vocabulary lists.   Build a simple user interface.   Methods  For this project I’m following domain-driven design (DDD), which is an approach where a domain model is at the center of the software. To ensure that my domain model is robust, I’m also applying test-driven design (TDD): writing failing tests first, and writing implementation to make the tests pass.  I’m writing my application in Java, as its object-oriented nature synergizes well with domain-driven design. I’m also using IntelliJ IDEA to write and execute my code.  Finally, in the spirit of agile development, I want to divide this project into manageable chunks, where I have a viable application at the end of each one. Even as a solo developer, that helps my sanity, and it has the added bonus of keeping these blog posts at a manageable level.  The code for my project is available on my Github. As a disclaimer, I will say that at the point of writing, I’ve already completed the first three parts of the project: constructing a console application, converting this application to Spring Boot, and using Spring Boot to construct a RESTful API. Therefore, my version history on GitHub might deviate from the order in which I’ve written these posts.  Except where explicitly specified, generative AI was not used for this project.
